title: Stacks
summary: Last in, first out: nested pairs, undo, and a depth-first walk.

parts.rule: A stack is last-in, first-out. Push and pop at one end in O(1). Use it when the most recent unfinished item must be resolved first: matching brackets, undo history, monotonic candidates, or an explicit depth-first walk that replaces recursion.
parts.why: Nested structure shows up in parsing and path problems. Recursion hides a call stack; an explicit stack makes the same idea interview-visible and avoids blowing the language call limit on deep inputs. The usual failures are popping when empty, forgetting that order reverses on the way out, and using a queue when newest-first is required.
parts.example: Validate "([]){}". Process left to right with an empty stack. See "(" → push. See "[" → push. See "]" → top is "[", characters match, pop. See ")" → top is "(", match, pop. See "{" → push. See "}" → top is "{", match, pop. Stack empty at end → valid. Counterexample "([)]": after pushing "(" then "[", the next character ")" wants an opening "(", but the top is "[", so reject immediately without scanning further. Same structure for maze undo: positions pushed as you walk; on a dead end pop and try the next unused neighbor. For next-greater on [2, 1, 3]: scan left to right with a monotonic decreasing stack of indices; when 3 arrives, pop 1 then 2, recording 3 as their next greater, then push 3.
parts.use: Use a stack for bracket and nest matching, calculator parsing, undo buffers, and converting recursion into an explicit loop. Use a monotonic stack when you need the previous greater or next smaller element in linear total time. Use it whenever the problem language says "innermost first" or "most recent unmatched."
parts.refuse: Refuse a stack when the order must be first-in, first-out — that is a queue. Refuse recursion-plus-stack double bookkeeping when one stack is enough. Refuse popping without an empty check. Refuse a stack as a general bag when you need random lookup of older entries that are not on top.

body:
Rule. A stack is last-in, first-out. Push and pop at one end in O(1). Use it when the most recent unfinished item must be resolved first: matching brackets, undo history, monotonic candidates, or an explicit depth-first walk that replaces recursion.

Why it matters. Nested structure shows up in parsing and path problems. Recursion hides a call stack; an explicit stack makes the same idea interview-visible and avoids blowing the language call limit on deep inputs. The usual failures are popping when empty, forgetting that order reverses on the way out, and using a queue when newest-first is required.

Worked example. Validate "([]){}". Process left to right with an empty stack. See "(" → push. See "[" → push. See "]" → top is "[", characters match, pop. See ")" → top is "(", match, pop. See "{" → push. See "}" → top is "{", match, pop. Stack empty at end → valid. Counterexample "([)]": after pushing "(" then "[", the next character ")" wants an opening "(", but the top is "[", so reject immediately without scanning further. Same structure for maze undo: positions pushed as you walk; on a dead end pop and try the next unused neighbor. For next-greater on [2, 1, 3]: scan left to right with a monotonic decreasing stack of indices; when 3 arrives, pop 1 then 2, recording 3 as their next greater, then push 3.

When to use. Use a stack for bracket and nest matching, calculator parsing, undo buffers, and converting recursion into an explicit loop. Use a monotonic stack when you need the previous greater or next smaller element in linear total time. Use it whenever the problem language says "innermost first" or "most recent unmatched."

When to refuse. Refuse a stack when the order must be first-in, first-out — that is a queue. Refuse recursion-plus-stack double bookkeeping when one stack is enough. Refuse popping without an empty check. Refuse a stack as a general bag when you need random lookup of older entries that are not on top.
